hookLine: East and West split, over authority and a word in the creed, with faults on both sides

cards: July, 1054. Constantinople's great church, Hagia Sophia, during the afternoon service. Three envoys from the pope in Rome, led by a cardinal named Humbert, walk up the aisle and lay a document on the altar.
It excommunicates the patriarch of Constantinople. Then they walk out, shaking the dust off their feet. A deacon runs after them, begging them to take it back.

They refuse. Days later the patriarch, Michael Cerularius, excommunicates the envoys in return. The strange part: the pope who sent them had already died, so some historians wonder whether the document even counted.
Nobody in that church could know what they were watching, or how long it would last.

teach.h: SCHISMA: A TEAR IN THE CLOTH.
teach.b: Schism comes from the Greek schisma, a tear, a rip in cloth. Jesus uses it in a saying about sewing new cloth onto an old coat: "the rent is made worse."
Paul begs the church at Corinth "that there be no divisions among you," the same word. So the Bible itself treats a schism as a wound. What tore in 1054?
Two things, mostly. First, authority. The bishop of Rome said he spoke for the whole church, as successor of Peter.
The Eastern bishops honored Rome as first among equals, but not as a ruler over them.

teach.h: AUTHORITY, AND ONE WORD IN THE CREED.
teach.b: Second, one word in the creed. Over the centuries, Western churches had added a Latin word, filioque, and the Son, to the line about the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father.

The East said nobody had the right to change a creed agreed at a council, and that the change blurred something true about God. Smaller quarrels too: leavened or unleavened bread, beards, fasting days.
Historians now say 1054 was less a single day than a long drifting apart: different languages, different empires, and neither side trying very hard to understand the other.
The worst blow came in 1204, when Western crusaders sacked Constantinople itself. There were faults on both sides, and churches on both sides now say so.
In 1965, Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras formally lifted the excommunications of 1054.

teach.h: THAT THERE BE NO DIVISIONS AMONG YOU.
teach.b: They didn't end the split. But they took the paper off the altar.

how: Catholic and Orthodox leaders now meet regularly, and every year on the feasts of Saint Andrew and of Saints Peter and Paul delegations from Rome and Constantinople visit each other to pray together.

practice: Think of a tear, in a family, a friendship, a church, something that split years ago and was never quite mended. Don't decide who was right; just notice where it still aches, and that both sides probably had a piece of the fault.
If you pray, pray for reconciliation, between East and West and in the tear you're thinking of; if you don't, hold both sides in mind at once, gently.

wordCard.voice: Schism. From the Greek for a tear in cloth. A split in the church, like the one between East and West.

orig.note: Greek: a tear or rip, as in cloth. Used in Mark 2:21 and 1 Corinthians 1:10.

carryVoice: Your line: the split still aches. Lifted is not the same as mended. See you tomorrow.
